bc_the_north_walls.blurb: The North Walls are the north-facing section of the Stawamus Chief granite dome above Squamish. All 23 climbs here are trad, mostly long free routes, with grades starting around 5.9 but clustering in the 5.11 and 5.12 range and a handful reaching 5.13 and 5.14. This is a place for experienced parties. The face stays cool when the rest of the Chief is baking, which helps in summer, but it dries slowly, has a shorter spring and fall window than its neighbours, and tends to be dirtier. A ledge splits the wall at mid-height, and many of the longer lines can be used to reach it from the ground.

bc_the_belfry.blurb: The Belfry is a steep sport wall in the Grand Canyon sector of Skaha Bluffs, a dry climbing park above Skaha Lake near Penticton. All 23 routes are bolted and nearly all are 5.11 or harder, with the bulk at 5.12 and 5.13 and a few at the very top end. Expect overhanging, technical, sustained climbing that feels closer to a gym than a typical crag, which makes it the hardest wall in its canyon and a poor pick for beginners. The wall is shaded in the morning and gets very hot through the afternoon, so plan the day around that in summer.
bc_the_belfry.approach: From the upper parking lot, take the upper trail and stay on the Grand Canyon trail past Diamondback, down the left side of the canyon through the base of The Terraces, then past Tottering Pillar and across the canyon to the wall.

bc_tottering_pillar.blurb: Tottering Pillar is a mid-canyon wall in the Grand Canyon sector of Skaha Bluffs, above Skaha Lake near Penticton. It holds 23 routes split fairly evenly between bolted and gear-protected lines, mostly vertical and technical, with the bulk at 5.11 and 5.12 and a few easier lines from 5.7 through 5.10. Most of the climbing is on the lower Bottom Line Wall rather than the pillar itself, whose base is loose and is usually reached by rappelling from above. Canyon walls on both sides let you choose sun or shade, and the walk in from the upper lot passes the base of The Terraces first.
bc_tottering_pillar.approach: From the upper parking lot, take the upper trail and stay on the Grand Canyon trail past Diamondback, then down the left side of the canyon through the base of The Terraces and on down the path to the pillar.

bc_shipwreck_boulders.blurb: Shipwreck Boulders, also known as The Happies, is one of two main zones at Cobbles Bouldering in the Fraser Valley. The blocks are big and steep, with scoops, pockets, edges and pinches rather than slopers or slabs, so the climbing is burly and powerful. Its 23 problems are mostly V3 to V5, with one easier problem and a top end of V8 and V9 for strong boulderers, so it is not a beginner venue. The other main zone, the Hotel Boulders, is about ten minutes' walk away, with more blocks scattered through the forest in between.

bc_the_buttress.blurb: The Buttress is the largest wall in the Eldred Valley, a remote granite area north of Powell River. It has 23 routes, split about evenly between bolted and trad lines with a single aid line, and the grades are mostly 5.11 and 5.12 with only a few easier ones. Many lines are multi-pitch. Low-angle corner systems climb to a steeper headwall, and the rock is regarded as cleaner than on many neighbouring walls. In midsummer the face stays shaded until about midday. The top is also a good viewpoint over the surrounding walls.

bc_edwin_wall.blurb: Edwin Wall is one of the main walls at Aberdeen Columns, a basalt crack-climbing area in the Okanagan hills near Vernon. It is the first wall you meet beyond the initial talus field, easy to pick out by its yellow colour, and it holds 22 routes, nearly all trad plus one aid line. Grades are friendly for a crack venue: mostly 5.8 through 5.10, with a single 5.11. The columnar basalt gives straight-in finger to offwidth cracks up to about 25 m tall, and the neighbouring section has some loose columns, so check holds on less-travelled lines.

bc_rossland_better_than_nothing.blurb: Better Than Nothing is a wooded crag of short routes near Rossland in the West Kootenay. Of its 22 routes, most are bolted and a few are trad, with grades from an easy 5.4 up to 5.11 but the bulk at 5.9 and 5.10, so it suits climbers working through the middle grades. The routes are short and generally well protected, and the forest setting makes it a pleasant first crag for younger climbers. Anchors are built for leading, so top-roping may call for long slings to keep drag down. Expect a damp walk in spring.
bc_rossland_better_than_nothing.approach: A walk of roughly 15 to 20 minutes from the end of the road to the crag; the trail is wet in spring.
